title: Abhijeet Dipke Launches School Audit Campaign From Native Maharashtra Village
excerpt: The Cockroach Janta Party founder, who returned from Boston to lead India's biggest youth protest in years, is now targeting rural school infrastructure with a nationwide citizen-led audit starting on Independence Day.
body:
• CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke is launching the "School Thik Karo" campaign on August 15, starting from his native village in Hingoli, Maharashtra
  • The nationwide social audit will ask parents and citizens to inspect government schools for basic facilities including functional toilets, drinking water and electricity
  • Dipke, a 30-year-old Boston University graduate who returned to India in June, previously led protests that forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign
  • The CJP's Instagram account has amassed over 22 million followers since its founding in May 2026

Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of India's viral Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement, is shifting his focus from exam reform to school infrastructure, launching a nationwide campaign to audit government schools in rural India. The campaign begins on August 15 — India's Independence Day — from his native village in Hingoli, Maharashtra, according to Livemint.

Dipke, 30, plans to meet the local Sarpanch and push for improvements at government schools in the area, where he has flagged issues including dirty, unusable toilets. "How can any kid use this?" he asked, pointing to the state of washrooms at a school in his home village, according to Hindustan Times.

From Boston to the Barricades

Dipke's trajectory from a Boston University graduate student to the face of India's largest youth protest movement has been swift. Born into a Dalit family in Aurangabad, Maharashtra, he moved to the U.S. in 2023 to pursue a master's in public relations, according to Reuters.

https://x.com/Cockroachisback/status/2088466295259816179

On May 16, 2026, he posted six words on X: "What if all cockroaches come together?" — a response to Supreme Court judge Surya Kant, who had compared unemployed youth to cockroaches during a hearing. The post went viral. Within days, the satirical Cockroach Janta Party had amassed millions of followers.

"This is a movement to change the political discourse of India. The youth of India has largely vanished from the mainstream political discourse."

— Abhijeet Dipke, CJP Founder (speaking to Reuters from Boston)

Dipke flew back to India in early June and set up a protest camp at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi. Tens of thousands gathered demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over leaked medical entrance exam papers that affected some 2 million students and were linked to several student suicides. Pradhan resigned in July — what Reuters described as "one of Modi's biggest defeats."

School Thik Karo: A Citizen-Led Audit

The new campaign asks parents, village leaders and ordinary citizens to inspect rural government schools and document the availability of basic facilities: electricity, drinking water, separate functional washrooms for boys and girls, and hygienic midday meals.

The CJP will provide a printable audit form through its social media channels. Citizens can record which facilities are present or missing and submit completed forms with video evidence. The organization plans to publish before-and-after photographs and publicly recognize Sarpanches who successfully upgrade their local schools.

"Every child of every citizen of India deserves a better tomorrow because quality education is a fundamental right," the campaign organizers said, according to Livemint.

A Movement That Won't Fade

The CJP's rise has drawn both support and scrutiny. CNN reported the government blocked the party's X account over what the Intelligence Bureau called "national security concerns." Education Minister Pradhan had called the movement the "B-team of terror groups" before his resignation. Activist Sonam Wangchuk and several opposition parties have backed the protests.

"The real India lives in its villages, and it is time our schools reflect that," Dipke said.

What's Next

Dipke's story resonates with the Indian diaspora — a young man who left for higher education in the U.S. and returned to challenge systemic failures at home. The School Thik Karo campaign represents a shift from protest to ground-level action, with the CJP positioning itself as a permanent watchdog for India's education system rather than a single-issue movement.

The campaign's August 15 launch from Hingoli is designed to be replicated by Sarpanches and citizens across the country. Whether the momentum translates into lasting infrastructure improvements remains the central question.
nri_angle: Dipke left India for a master's degree in Boston and returned to lead a youth movement challenging systemic failures in education.
